opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes from caring a lot about the work, and about the people doing it. In research, especially at the frontier, the standard isn't set by us. It's set by the world. If a paper or a model goes out and it isn't good enough, reviewers will tell you, users will tell you, competitors will simply move past you. So I'd rather the team hear the hard truth from me, early, in a room where we can still fix things, than hear it later from the outside when it's too late.

When I look at a result, I try to ask the questions a very skeptical person would ask. Is this baseline fair? Is this improvement real, or is it noise? Would someone actually want to use this? Sometimes that comes across as stern, because I don't soften it very much. I'm direct. But I try to make it about the work, never about the person. I'm not saying "you're not good." I'm saying "this isn't there yet, and here's why."

I've also learned that people actually grow the most when the bar is high and clear. When I was younger, the mentors who helped me most weren't the ones who said everything was great. They were the ones who pushed back, who made me redo experiments, who asked why I made a certain choice. At the time it didn't feel pleasant, but looking back, that's where I learned how to do research properly.

That said, I've had to reflect on it. Sternness only works if there's trust. If people don't believe you're on their side, harsh feedback just makes them defensive or afraid, and fear kills creativity. So I try to balance it. I give credit generously when something is genuinely good, I try to explain my reasoning instead of just saying no, and I try to stay open to being wrong, because many times the junior researcher sees something I missed. The goal isn't to be tough. The goal is to make something we can all be proud of.

r001.rationale: The candidate says direct feedback can come across as stern and that trust affects how it works, but does not clearly say that the listener’s interpretation determines whether it is perceived as stern.

r002.rationale: The candidate says mentors who pushed back helped most, showing that candid feedback can be valued, but does not explain that people willing to identify improvements are uncommon.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the sternness people see in me comes from a very specific place, and it's not that I enjoy being harsh. It comes from taking the work seriously, and taking the person seriously.

When I give feedback, I'm usually looking at a result, not a person. If an experiment is poorly designed, or a claim in a paper is not supported, I will say so directly. I don't soften it much, because I think vague feedback is actually a form of disrespect. It wastes the other person's time. If I say "this is interesting, maybe consider some other baselines," the student walks away not knowing whether the work is fundamentally fine or fundamentally broken. If I say "this comparison is unfair and the conclusion doesn't hold," that's uncomfortable for a minute, but now they know exactly where they stand and what to fix.

Part of this is how I was trained. In my own PhD years, and later working in research labs, the feedback culture I grew up in was very direct. You present, people tear the idea apart, and if the idea survives, you know it's real. I came to see that process as a gift. The people who were hardest on my work were the ones who made me a better researcher. So in some sense I'm passing on what worked for me.

But I've also had to learn that sternness only works when there is trust underneath it. If someone doesn't believe that I want them to succeed, then direct criticism just feels like an attack. So I try to be very clear that my standard is high because I think they can reach it. I'm not stern with people I've given up on. I'm stern with people I expect a lot from.

And honestly, in a field moving this fast, with generative models and simulation and physical AI, there isn't a lot of room for comfortable illusions. If something doesn't work, the world will tell you eventually. I'd rather be the one who tells you first, in the lab, when it's still cheap to fix.

So I don't think of it as being tough. I think of it as being honest at a speed that matches the problem.

r001.rationale: The candidate says direct criticism feels like an attack if someone does not believe he wants them to succeed, while trust makes sternness work. This communicates that its reception depends on the listener’s interpretation.

r002.rationale: The candidate says direct feedback was a gift and helped him improve, but does not explain that candid feedback is appreciated because people who identify opportunities for improvement are uncommon.

astra-6.text:
I think my sternness comes from caring a lot about the work and wanting to be clear when something isn’t good enough. But that doesn’t automatically make the way I deliver feedback right. I have to separate the standard I’m asking for from my own impatience.

Ideally, someone should leave that conversation understanding what needs to improve and why, and feeling able to challenge my reasoning. If they leave only knowing that I’m unhappy, then I haven’t really done my job. I want to be demanding about the work while still giving people room to think, disagree, and make mistakes.

But having high standards doesn’t automatically make the way I communicate effective. I need to explain why something matters, listen to the other person’s reasoning, and make sure the feedback gives them a way forward. The standard can be demanding while the conversation remains respectful.
